\chapter{Who, When, Where, How Many}
\label{ch:pa-question-words}
\hlchaptermodality{43}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask who, when, where and how many, and hear that the question family, the clause that answers it and the word that points at the answer are three parallel series.}

The question family completed, and the pattern under it: ka- asks, ja- opens the clause that answers, o- points at what it means. kadon and jadon differ by exactly one letter, so the answer taught two chapters earlier turns out to have been half of a pair. kaun had been NAMED once, in a romanised aside, and never written in Gurmukhi -- a different kind of gap from the merely absent. kitthe is the only word in seven chapters that needed a new letter, and the writing lesson that buys it says so.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kauṇ]{\pa{ਕੌਣ} (kauṇ) — who}

\label{lesson:PA-C43-kaun}



\begin{quote}
From the chapter behind you, the describing pair. From the \emph{kivēṁ} lesson, the question word that named the family. And from three chapters back, \emph{why}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{jo … oh …}, \emph{kivēṁ}, \emph{kyoṁ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{je} — from two chapters back
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{ate} — from five chapters back, cold
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਕੌਣ}} — \emph{kauṇ} — \textbf{who}
\end{quote}

The same \textbf{\pa{ਕ}} as every question word. This one has an odd history in this book: it was \textbf{named once}, in a romanised aside about the family, in Latin letters — never written in Gurmukhi, never practised, never a word you owned.

That is a different kind of gap from the missing ones. The book told you it existed and never handed it over.

Now hold the two families side by side, because they answer each other:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਕ}-} asks · \textbf{\pa{ਜ}-} opens the clause that answers · \textbf{\pa{ਉ}-} points at it
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kauṇ?} — flat, as a whole question.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{kauṇ?} and \emph{kyoṁ?} — a person, a reason.
  \item \emph{Run through:} ask \emph{kauṇ?} and answer with a \textbf{\pa{ਜੋ}} clause.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask \emph{who}. What do \textbf{\pa{ਕ}-}, \textbf{\pa{ਜ}-} and \textbf{\pa{ਉ}-} each do? (Ask, open the answering clause, point at what it means.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kadoṁ]{\pa{ਕਦੋਂ} (kadoṁ) — when}

\label{lesson:PA-C43-kadon}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, \emph{who}. Two chapters back, the word that places one event against another.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{kauṇ}, and \emph{jadoṁ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{je … tāṁ …} — from two chapters back
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{ate} joining two sentences — from five chapters back, cold
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Put them side by side. This is the neatest pattern in the chapter:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਕਦੋਂ}} — \emph{when?} · \textbf{\pa{ਜਦੋਂ}} — \emph{when …}
\end{quote}

\textbf{One letter apart.} The \textbf{\pa{ਕ}} asks; the \textbf{\pa{ਜ}} answers. You learned the answer two chapters ago without knowing it was half of a pair, and the question costs you almost nothing now.

That pairing runs through the whole language, and you have now seen it three times: \textbf{\pa{ਜੇ} … \pa{ਤਾਂ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਜੋ} … \pa{ਉਹ}}, and now \textbf{\pa{ਕਦੋਂ}} against \textbf{\pa{ਜਦੋਂ}}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{kadoṁ?} and \emph{jadoṁ} — question, then answer.
  \item \emph{Run through:} ask \emph{kadoṁ?}, then answer with a \emph{jadoṁ} clause.
  \item \emph{Say it:} the three fronts in a row — \emph{ka-}, \emph{ja-}, \emph{o-}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask \emph{when}, then answer it. What single letter separates the two words? (The first — \textbf{\pa{ਕ}} asks, \textbf{\pa{ਜ}} answers.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tha]{\pa{ਥ} — the consonant tha}

\label{lesson:PA-W10-thatha}



\begin{quote}
One chapter back you wrote \textbf{\pa{ਉਹ}}. Write it once from memory.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — one new form, and why it is here}
Keep \textbf{\pa{ਥ}} visible beside \textbf{\pa{ਤ}}, which you have had for a long time:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\pa{ਤ}} — \emph{ta}, the plain dental · \textbf{\pa{ਥ}} — \emph{tha}, the same place with a push of
  \item breath behind it
\end{itemize}

The tongue is in the same spot for both; the difference is the breath. Say \emph{ta} with your hand in front of your mouth, then \emph{tha}, and feel it.

Worth saying plainly, because it is the point of this whole run of chapters: \textbf{this is the only new letter in seven chapters.} Every joining word — \emph{ate}, \emph{jāṁ}, \emph{par}, \emph{lekin}, \emph{ki}, \emph{kyoṁki}, \emph{je}, \emph{jadoṁ}, \emph{jo}, \emph{laī} — was already writable with signs this book taught long ago. The words were missing; the script was not. One question needed one letter, and here it is.

\subsection*{Writing — notice and trace}
Finger-trace \textbf{\pa{ਥ}} once, then trace it once in the air. Say \emph{tha} with the breath audible as your finger finishes.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy, model in view}
Keep the model in view and copy \textbf{\pa{ਥ}} once, then \textbf{\pa{ਤ}} beside it. Repair only the stroke that separates them.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \textbf{\pa{ਤ}} and \textbf{\pa{ਥ}} carries the breath? (\textbf{\pa{ਥ}}.) How many new letters have these seven chapters spent? (This one.)

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \textbf{\pa{ਜੇ}} written — from two chapters back
  \item \emph{Recall:} \textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}} written — from five chapters back, cold
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kitthe]{\pa{ਕਿੱਥੇ} (kitthe) — where}

\label{lesson:PA-C43-kitthe}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, the new letter. And the two questions this chapter has already given you.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\pa{ਥ}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{kauṇ}, \emph{kadoṁ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{jadoṁ} — from two chapters back
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{jāṁ} — from five chapters back, cold
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਕਿੱਥੇ}} — \emph{kitthe} — \textbf{where}
\end{quote}

Read it in pieces: \textbf{\pa{ਕ}}, the \textbf{\pa{ਿ}} sihari before it, the \textbf{\pa{ੱ}} addak that doubles the next sound, then \textbf{\pa{ਥ}} — new one lesson ago — and the \textbf{\pa{ੇ}} laav.

The addak is doing real work. It doubles the \textbf{\pa{ਥ}}, which is why the word is \emph{kit-the} and not \emph{ki-the}. Leave it off and the word loses its middle.

This is the question that asks where somebody lives, and asking that is most of what a spoken interview at this level is for. The book has taught house, city and village for many chapters and could not ask where any of them was.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kitthe?} with the doubled \emph{th} audible.
  \item \emph{Build:} ask where somebody lives.
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\pa{ਕਿੱਥੇ}}, model in view, and check the addak.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask where someone lives. What does the \textbf{\pa{ੱ}} do, and what happens if you leave it out? (Doubles the \textbf{\pa{ਥ}}; the word loses its middle.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kinne]{\pa{ਕਿੰਨੇ} (kinne) — how many}

\label{lesson:PA-C43-kinne}



\begin{quote}
The three questions this chapter has given you so far. Say them in order.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{kauṇ}, \emph{kadoṁ}, \emph{kitthe}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{laī} — from two chapters back
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{nā … nā …} — from five chapters back, cold
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਕਿੰਨੇ}} — \emph{kinne} — \textbf{how many}, \textbf{how much}
\end{quote}

The same \textbf{\pa{ਕ}} one last time, now asking about quantity. With it the family this book named when it taught \emph{kivēṁ} is finally complete on the page:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\pa{ਕੀ}} what · \textbf{\pa{ਕਿਵੇਂ}} how · \textbf{\pa{ਕਿਉਂ}} why · \textbf{\pa{ਕੌਣ}} who · \textbf{\pa{ਕਦੋਂ}} when ·
  \item \textbf{\pa{ਕਿੱਥੇ}} where · \textbf{\pa{ਕਿੰਨੇ}} how many
\end{itemize}

Two of those you had before this run. Five arrived in the last four chapters, and only one of the five cost a new letter.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kinne?} — flat, as a whole question.
  \item \emph{Run through:} the whole family in a row, one breath each.
  \item \emph{Build:} ask how many of something you can name.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask all the questions you know, in one run. What do they share, and where were you first told so? (The opening \textbf{\pa{ਕ}}; the \emph{kivēṁ} lesson.)
